title: Story-Based Interviews
intro: Ask for one specific, recent story. Opinions about the future aren’t data.

learn.title: Why stories
learn.text:
“Would you use this?” invites a guess.
“Tell me about the last time you…” brings back what happened.

The details of a real story make the who, what, why and how trustworthy.

options: Tell me about the last time you exported a report
Would you use a faster export?
How often do you usually export?
What would your ideal export look like if you could design it?
try.explain: It anchors the answer in one real event.

learn.title: Dig it out
learn.text:
**Set the scene:** when, where, what happened just before.
**Keep them in the moment;** ask what happened next.
**Bring generalisations back:** “I usually…” → “And last time?”
**Don’t stop at a short answer.**

try.q: They say “I usually check it every morning.” Best follow-up?
options: And the last time you checked it, what happened?
Why do you check it every morning?
Would you like us to send you a daily summary instead of that?
How long does that usually take you?

learn.title: Three kinds of bad data
learn.text:
**Compliments:** “That’s really cool.”
**Generalisations and promises:** “I always…”, “I would definitely buy that.”
**Feature requests:** “You should add…”

Each is a prompt to dig, not evidence.

try.q: “I would definitely buy that.” What is it?
options: A future promise, the least reliable data
Strong evidence of demand you can plan the roadmap around
A sign to start building
A useful price signal
try.explain: Ask what they do today and what it costs them.

learn.title: Commitment
learn.text:
When you’re testing demand, interest shows as something given up:
**time** (a trial, another meeting), **reputation** (an introduction), **money** (a pre-order).

Compliments and no next step taught you little.

options: They introduce you to their manager
They say the idea is brilliant
They promise to try it as soon as it launches someday
They ask for more features

learn.title: Make it weekly
learn.text:
**Recruit automatically:** an in-product invite, a line in onboarding.
**Interview as a trio.**
**Write a snapshot within the hour:** a quote, quick facts, the story’s moments, the opportunities heard.

try.q: What goes in an interview snapshot?
options: A quote, the story’s moments, the opportunities
A full transcript of the whole interview, word for word
A feature list for the roadmap
A score for the participant
try.explain: One page, written while the story is fresh.

test.q: Why ask about the past rather than the future?
options: People can’t predict what they’ll do
Past questions are quicker to answer
Future questions upset participants
Past behaviour is easier to quantify
test.explain: Predictions are guesses; stories are facts.

test.q: Instead of “How much would you pay?”, ask:
options: What did this problem cost you last month?
Would you pay a monthly fee for it?
Is our planned price higher or lower than you expected it to be?
Which price tier would you choose?
test.explain: Real costs reveal what solving it is worth.

test.q: A participant suggests a feature. What next?
options: Ask why they want it and what they do now
Add it to the backlog straight away, with their name attached
Explain why it can’t be built
Ask them to rank it against others
test.explain: The need underneath is the opportunity.

test.q: Which is a commitment of money?
options: A pre-order paid in advance
A positive review
A second interview
An introduction to a colleague
test.explain: Money, time and reputation are the three kinds.

test.q: What is the classic interviewer mistake?
options: Selling when you should be listening
Asking too many follow-up questions
Taking detailed notes during the interview itself
Interviewing with a colleague
test.explain: If you hear yourself explaining the product, switch back to their story.

test.q: When should the snapshot be written?
options: Within the hour
At the end of the week
After all interviews are done
Before the next planning cycle
